in-protoreaster-nodosus.title: Chocolate Chip Sea Star
in-protoreaster-nodosus.summary: A sea star named for its dark "chocolate chip" knobs. Hardy for a sea star but not reef safe.
rows: About 1' 3 in; wild record 30 cm (11.8 in) across (SeaLifeBase)
No. Adults eat soft corals, sponges, tubeworms and clams
Carnivore. Meaty foods; adults also eat sessile invertebrates
Indo-West Pacific: from Seychelles to Australia and Japan
notes: Needs high water quality and does not tolerate high nitrate.
Wants a large tank with a mature sand bed several inches deep; keep away from triggers and puffers.

in-linckia-laevigata.title: Blue Linckia Starfish
in-linckia-laevigata.summary: A bright blue Indo-Pacific sea star that grazes detritus and films off rock. Reef safe but hard to keep alive long term; only for large, mature tanks.
rows: Up to about 12 in (30 cm) across
Grazes detritus, algae films and small organisms on rock and sand; may not take offered food
notes: Needs a large, mature tank with lots of live rock to graze.

in-tripneustes-ventricosus.title: Short Spine Urchin (West Indian Sea Egg)
in-tripneustes-ventricosus.summary: A Caribbean urchin with a dark body and short white spines that grazes algae, including hair algae. It wanders and moves loose rock and corals.
rows: About 4 in (10 cm) across; up to about 6 in in the wild
About 106 gallons, with sand and coralline algae
Mostly: it can knock over or move loose corals and rocks
Algae grazer: film and hair algae, plus nori and other seaweed if algae runs short
notes: Glue down frags and secure loose rock.

in-diadema-savignyi.title: Blue Eye Long Spine Urchin (Savigny's Urchin)
in-diadema-savignyi.summary: A black urchin with very long, sharp spines and blue markings. It grazes algae, mostly at night, and needs a roomy tank with rock cover and careful handling.
rows: Body about 4 in; spines 10–12 in (up to about 10 in tip to tip in the wild)
Algae grazer, most active at night; needs a tank with steady algae growth
Indo-Pacific: East Africa to the South Pacific islands and Japan
warn: Long, sharp spines cause painful puncture wounds: handle with care.

in-oreasteridae-sea-star.title: Knobbed Sea Star (Pentaceraster)
in-oreasteridae-sea-star.summary: A thick-bodied, knobby sea star from warm Pacific and Indian Ocean coasts. Knobbed sea stars like this are best kept away from soft corals, clams and tubeworms.
rows: No: related knobbed sea stars eat soft corals, tubeworms and clams
Omnivore: detritus, algae and dead matter; needs sand, rock and algae to forage
Warm coastal waters of the Pacific and Indian Oceans
notes: Acclimate slowly and keep water stable: sea stars are very sensitive to water quality.
Do not keep with predatory fish.

in-linckia-multiflora.title: Multicolor Linckia Sea Star
in-linckia-multiflora.summary: A slender, mottled sea star that grazes film and microbes off rock. Reef safe, but it needs a mature tank and very stable water.
rows: 25 gal or larger, established at least a year
Grazer: bacterial film, algae and sponges on live rock; extra feeding rarely needed in a mature tank
Indo-Pacific: lagoons, reef flats and seaward reefs
notes: Acclimate slowly (2+ hours) and keep water stable.

in-linckia-red.title: Red Linckia Sea Star
in-linckia-red.summary: A smooth red sea star that grazes film off rock. Reef safe, but sensitive to changes in water quality.
rows: Grazer: film and microbes on live rock
notes: Keep pH, salinity and temperature steady; swings can lead to infections.

in-eucidaris-tribuloides.title: Pencil Urchin (Slate Pencil Urchin)
in-eucidaris-tribuloides.summary: A hardy Atlantic urchin with thick, blunt, mildly venomous spines. It scavenges algae and detritus at night and hides in crevices by day.
rows: Yes, with caution: it can trample corals
Omnivore: mostly algae and detritus, plus supplemental feedings
Western Atlantic (North Carolina to Brazil) and eastern Atlantic; reefs, seagrass and rocky bottoms

in-astropecten-sand-star.title: Sand Sifting Sea Star
in-astropecten-sand-star.summary: A flat, spiny-edged sea star that burrows through the sand cleaning up detritus. It needs plenty of sand and stable salinity.
rows: 10 gal minimum; larger sand beds are much better
Scavenger: detritus and debris it sifts from the sand
notes: Needs plenty of sand to search.

in-echinometra-lucunter.title: Rock Boring Urchin
in-echinometra-lucunter.summary: A small black to reddish-brown Caribbean urchin with short, sharp spines. In the wild it wedges into holes in shallow, wave-washed rock and grazes algae.
rows: 20 gal or larger with stable rockwork
With caution: its spines can knock over frags or scrape corals, and it may graze coralline algae
Algae grazer: microalgae, diatoms and detritus; supplement with algae sheets
Western Atlantic: Florida and the Caribbean to Brazil
notes: Handle carefully: the spines are sharp.
warn: Sensitive to copper and to salinity changes; acclimate slowly.
